fields.statement: Let $d\ge1$ be an integer, let $f:\mathbb R^d\to\overline{\mathbb R}$ be closed, proper, and convex, and let $p\in\mathbb R^d$. Define $g(x)=f(x)-\langle p,x\rangle$. Assume $g$ is **coercive**, meaning that for every $M\in\mathbb R$ there is $R>0$ such that $\|x\|_2\ge R$ implies $g(x)>M$. Then $g$ has a finite global minimum at some $x_*\in\operatorname{dom}f$. The supremum defining $f^*(p)$ is finite and attained at $x_*$, and $p\in\partial f(x_*)$. No uniqueness is asserted.

Let $m\ge1$ and $d\ge1$ be integers, let $q_1,\ldots,q_m\in\mathbb R^d$, and let $a_1,\ldots,a_m\in\mathbb R$. Put

$$\Delta_m=\{\theta\in\mathbb R^m:\theta_i\ge0,\ \sum_{i=1}^m\theta_i=1\},\qquad P:=\left\{\sum_{i=1}^m\theta_iq_i:\theta\in\Delta_m\right\}.$$

Thus $P$ is the finite convex hull of the listed points, defined here as their convex combinations.

For $x\in P$ let $\Theta_x=\{\theta\in\Delta_m:\sum_i\theta_iq_i=x\}$ and define

$$f_{\rm mix}(x)=\min_{\theta\in\Theta_x}\sum_{i=1}^m\theta_i a_i;$$

set $f_{\rm mix}(x)=+\infty$ for $x\notin P$. Then every minimum is attained; $f_{\rm mix}$ is proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex; and it is pointwise greatest among convex functions $h:\mathbb R^d\to\overline{\mathbb R}$ satisfying $h(q_i)\le a_i$ for every $i$. Consequently $f_{\rm mix}=f_{\rm mix}^{**}$. If $p\in\partial f_{\rm mix}(x)$ and $\theta$ is any minimizing mixture for $x$, then every $i$ with $\theta_i>0$ satisfies

$$a_i=\langle p,q_i\rangle-f_{\rm mix}^*(p).$$

Thus all occupied data points $(q_i,a_i)$ lie on one supporting affine hyperplane. The assertion is finite-dimensional and makes no claim about infinite families.

Assume the strict-reference representation conclusion of the draft supplier [[thm-tdmath-additive-entropy-representation]] for its nonempty state set $X$ and stated comparison hypotheses. Let $d\ge1$ and $m\ge1$ be integers, and take a finite list of distinct states $s_1,\ldots,s_m\in X$. Let $q_1,\ldots,q_m\in\mathbb R^d$ and set $a_i:=S(s_i)$ for $1\le i\le m$. Let $e_s$ be the unit-state compound defined in [[def-tdmath-tagged-scalable-compound]]; it is a mass-one point mass by [[lem-tdmath-compound-mass-well-defined]]. For $\theta\in\Delta_m$, put $M_\theta=\sum_i\theta_i e_{s_i}$ and set $V(\theta):=\sum_i\theta_iS(s_i)$. Suppose a map $\chi:\{M_\theta:\theta\in\Delta_m\}\to\mathbb R^d$ satisfies $\chi(M_\theta)=\sum_i\theta_iq_i$ for every $\theta\in\Delta_m$. For each $x\in\mathbb R^d$, define the value to be $+\infty$ if no $\theta\in\Delta_m$ has coordinate $x$. Then the minimum represented value among those finite mixtures, with that empty-feasible-set convention, is exactly the finite-mixture envelope $f_{\rm mix}(x)$ of [[thm-tdmath-finite-mixture-envelope]], with all its attainment, convexity, lower-semicontinuity, biconjugation, and supporting-face conclusions. This is the complete conditional transfer under the representation conclusion and affine coordinate assignment; the supplier definition and mass-one fact are provided locally.

Use $\mathbb N$ from [[def-natural-numbers]], which includes $0$, and define $\mathbb N_{>0}:=\mathbb N\setminus\{0\}$. A **finite-state thermodynamic-limit contract** specifies a sequence $(X_k,E_k,g_k,V_k,n_k)_{k\in\mathbb N_{>0}}$, where each $X_k$ is a finite nonempty state set, $E_k:X_k\to\mathbb R$ assigns finite energies in joules, $g_k:X_k\to(0,\infty)$ assigns positive dimensionless weights, $V_k>0$ is physical volume in $\mathrm{m^3}$, and, for one declared species, $n_k>0$ is its amount in moles. A fixed-density sequence has $V_k\to\infty$ and $n_k/V_k\to\rho\in(0,\infty)$ in $\mathrm{mol\,m^{-3}}$. Boundary conditions, interaction rules, and the choice of a volume or amount normalization are part of the contract and must be held fixed or explicitly tracked as $k$ varies.

For $T>0$, set $\beta:=(k_BT)^{-1}$ in $\mathrm{J^{-1}}$, with $k_B$ and units from [[def-td-si-quantities]]. The finite-state canonical partition sum is

$$
Z_k(\beta):=\sum_{x\in X_k}g_k(x)e^{-\beta E_k(x)},
$$

as the finite case of [[def-tdmath-countable-canonical-model]]. It is a positive finite real number. Define $F_k(\beta):=-\beta^{-1}\log Z_k(\beta)$ in joules and $f_k(\beta):=F_k(\beta)/V_k$ in $\mathrm{J\,m^{-3}}$. The specified thermodynamic-limit value is $f(\beta,\rho):=\lim_{k\to\infty} f_k(\beta)$ **if this limit exists**. A limit per mole or per lattice site is a different normalization and must be stated separately.

This is a contract for what a limit claim must specify, not a theorem that the limit exists. It asserts no uniformity in $\beta$, derivative interchange, ensemble equivalence, convergence rate, or nonanalyticity. A finite model's regularity and any limiting singularity require their own arguments; neither is inferred from the word “thermodynamic limit.”

A finite rate model consists of a finite nonempty state set $S$ and rates $q_{ij}\ge0$ in seconds$^{-1}$ for $i
e j$. Set $q_{ii}=-\sum_{j
e i}q_{ij}$. A row probability vector is $p=(p_i)_{i\in S}$ with $p_i\ge0$ and $\sum_i p_i=1$; write $\Delta(S)=\{p\in[0,1]^S:\sum_i p_i=1\}$. A time-dependent law is a coordinatewise continuously differentiable map $p:[0,\infty)	o\Delta(S)$, with a right derivative at $t=0$, that satisfies the continuous-time master equation $\dot p_i(t)=\sum_{j
e i}[p_j(t)q_{ji}-p_i(t)q_{ij}]$ for every $t\ge0$. A strictly positive normalized vector $\pi$ is a detailed-balance law when $\pi_iq_{ij}=\pi_jq_{ji}$ for every distinct pair. Its undirected rate graph has an edge $\{i,j\}$ exactly when $\pi_iq_{ij}>0$; detailed balance makes this equivalent to $\pi_jq_{ji}>0$.

On a finite nonempty state set $S$, a discrete transition kernel is a matrix $K:S	imes S	o[0,1]$ satisfying $\sum_{j\in S}K(i,j)=1$ for every $i\in S$. For a strictly positive row probability vector $\pi\in\Delta(S)$, the kernel satisfies $\pi$-detailed balance when $\pi_iK(i,j)=\pi_jK(j,i)$ for every $i,j\in S$. This identity pairs the supports of forward and reversed transitions. A rate model or a reversible kernel is a mathematical/physical model class; no observed trajectory is asserted by the definition.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $(M,\omega)$ be a smooth $2n$-dimensional symplectic manifold and $H\in C^\infty(M,\mathbb R)$, with Hamiltonian field defined by $\iota_{X_H}\omega=dH$. Wherever its local flow $\phi_t$ is defined, it preserves the symplectic form and the volume measure $m$ determined by $\omega^n/n!$. No completeness is asserted. Let $R$ be a measurable region invariant under a nonzero-time map $T=\phi_\tau$, so $T$ restricts to a self-map $R\to R$; then this restriction preserves the volume measure $m|_R$. If $m(R)<\infty$, then for every measurable $E\subseteq R$, almost every point of $E$ returns to $E$ infinitely often under forward iteration.

If $m(R)=1$ and $T$ is ergodic, then for every $f\in L^1(R,m)$ the averages $N^{-1}\sum_{j=0}^{N-1}f(T^jx)$ converge almost everywhere and in $L^1$ to $\int_Rf\,dm$. Without ergodicity, the limit is the invariant conditional expectation supplied by Birkhoff's theorem, not necessarily the space mean. Finally, if each stated time map $\phi_t$ is a diffeomorphism of a finite invariant region $R$, a density $p_0\ge0$ with $\int_Rp_0\,dm=1$ and $\int_R|p_0\log p_0|\,dm<\infty$ transports by $p_t=p_0\circ\phi_{-t}$ with conserved fine-grained entropy $-k_B\int_Rp_t\log p_t\,dm$, using $0\log0=0$. Volume preservation alone does not imply ergodicity or a time-average/ensemble identity.

Fix periods $L_1,\ldots,L_d>0$, let $\Omega=\prod_{j=1}^d(\mathbb R/L_j\mathbb Z)$ with quotient Lebesgue measure $dr$, let $d\ge2$, and let $I\subset\mathbb R$ be an open time interval. Suppose $f:\Omega	imes\mathbb R^d	imes I	o(0,\infty)$ is $C^1$ in space and time and $C^2$ in velocity. Fix a positive constant reference density $f_{m ref}$ with the same units as $f$, and put $\ell(r,v,t)=\log(f(r,v,t)/f_{m ref})$. For each $t\in I$, assume $f$, $f|v|^2$, and $f|\ell|$ are integrable over $\Omega	imes\mathbb R^d$. For every compact interval $I_0\subset I$, assume there is a nonnegative $G_{I_0}\in L^1(\Omega	imes\mathbb R^d,dr\,dv)$ such that $|(1+\ell)\partial_t f|\le G_{I_0}$ almost everywhere for every $t\in I_0$. Also assume $(1+|\ell|)|v\cdot
abla_r f|\in L^1(\Omega	imes\mathbb R^d,dr\,dv)$ for each $t\in I$. Write $A=f(r,v,t)f(r,w,t)$ and $B=f(r,v',t)f(r,w',t)$. For each $t\in I$, assume $r\mapsto\int_{Q_{m el}}|(A-B)(\ell(r,v,t)+\ell(r,w,t)-\ell(r,v',t)-\ell(r,w',t))|\,d
u$ is measurable and belongs to $L^1(\Omega,dr)$. Let $Q$ and the symmetric collision measure $
u$ satisfy the weak identity in [[def-tdmath-elastic-collision-kernel]] for tests $1$ and $\ell(r,\cdot,t)$ at each $(r,t)$, with absolute convergence, and suppose
$$\partial_t f+v\cdot
abla_r f=Q(f).$$
Then for $H[f](t)=\int_\Omega\int_{\mathbb R^d}f\ell\,dv\,dr$,
$$ rac{d}{dt}H[f](t)=- rac14\int_\Omega\int_{Q_{m el}}(A-B)\log(A/B)\,d
u\,dr\le0.$$
The integrand is nonnegative because $\log$ is strictly increasing. Equality in the entropy-production integral holds exactly when $A=B$ for $
u$-almost every collision at almost every $r$. Under the additional assumptions that $
u$ is locally finite, has full support on $Q_{m el}$, and $f$ is positive and $C^2$ in $v$, this balance implies for almost every $r$ that
$$\log(f(r,v,t)/f_{m ref})=\alpha(r,t)+b(r,t)\cdot v+ rac{\lambda(r,t)}2|v|^2.$$
If $f(r,\cdot,t)$ is integrable over $\mathbb R^d$, then $\lambda(r,t)<0$, so its velocity profile is Maxwellian. Conversely, every profile of this form has zero collision entropy production. The weak collision identity is an explicit model hypothesis; this is not a derivation from reversible many-particle mechanics or a PDE existence theorem.

Assume AC. Let $n\ge1$, let $O\subset\mathbb R^{2n}$ be open with its canonical symplectic form, let $H\in C^2(O,\mathbb R)$, and let $J\subset\mathbb R$ be open. Suppose $\nabla H\ne0$ on $H^{-1}(J)$ and $H^{-1}(K)$ is compact in $O$ for every compact $K\subset J$. Define $\mu_E$ by [[def-tdmath-regular-energy-shell]]. Then for every nonnegative Borel $f$ compactly supported in $H^{-1}(J)$,
$$\int_Of(x)\,dx=\int_J\mu_E(f)\,dE.$$
For every $E\in J$ with nonempty shell $\Sigma_E=H^{-1}(\{E\})$, $0<\mu_E(1)<\infty$, and $\widehat\mu_E=\mu_E/\mu_E(1)$ is a probability measure. Let $\phi_t$ be a Hamiltonian flow map defined as a diffeomorphism on a full compact energy band containing $\Sigma_E$ and preserving that band. Then $\widehat\mu_E$ is invariant under $\phi_t$ for every such regular $E$. Critical levels and noncompact bands are outside this statement.

Assume the Axiom of Choice [[def-axiom-of-choice]]. Assume the filtered probability space, Brownian increment hypothesis, and initial data of [[def-tdmath-ornstein-uhlenbeck-equation]], including $\mathbb E X_0^2<\infty$ and future increments independent of $\mathcal F_0$. For $\gamma,\sigma>0$, on every finite time interval the process
$$X_t=e^{-\gamma t}X_0+\sigma e^{-\gamma t}\int_0^t e^{\gamma s}\,dB_s$$
has a continuous adapted version, solves the stated Ornstein–Uhlenbeck integral equation, and is the unique continuous solution driven by the same $(X_0,B)$. Put $V=\sigma^2/(2\gamma)$. For $0\le s<t$, its transition law conditional on $\mathcal F_s$ is normal with mean $e^{-\gamma(t-s)}X_s$ and variance $V(1-e^{-2\gamma(t-s)})$. Consequently
$$\mathbb E X_t=e^{-\gamma t}\mathbb E X_0,\qquad\operatorname{Var}(X_t)=e^{-2\gamma t}\operatorname{Var}(X_0)+V(1-e^{-2\gamma t}).$$
From any such initial law, $X_t$ converges in distribution to $N(0,V)$. If $X_0\sim N(0,V)$ and is independent of future Brownian increments, the process is stationary Gaussian with covariance $C(\tau)=Ve^{-\gamma|\tau|}$, and its transition kernel satisfies detailed balance with the $N(0,V)$ density. Its transition density solves the Fokker–Planck equation for positive time. Under the convention $S(\omega)=(2\pi)^{-1}\int_{\mathbb R}C(\tau)e^{i\omega\tau}\,d\tau$, the stationary spectrum and time-average bound are
$$S(\omega)=\frac{V\gamma}{\pi(\gamma^2+\omega^2)},\qquad\operatorname{Var}\!\left(\frac1T\int_0^T X_t\,dt\right)\le\frac{2V}{\gamma T}.$$
All these statements concern the specified linear stochastic model. An Einstein relation between $\sigma$ and a physical bath temperature would be an additional physical postulate.
fields.proof:
**Given:** The Axiom of Choice, [A1]–[A2], and [F1]–[F7].

1.1 On $[0,T]$, $g(s)=e^{\gamma s}$ is deterministic, continuous, and square-integrable. Thus $W_t=\int_0^t g(s)\,dB_s$ is defined by [F3], and [F4] supplies a continuous version. For a partition $0=t_0<\cdots<t_n=t$, the deterministic step sums $\sum_k g(t_k)(B_{t_{k+1}}-B_{t_k})$ converge in $L^2$ to $W_t$ by the Itô isometry and uniform approximation of $g$. Discrete summation by parts rewrites them as $g(t)B_t-g(0)B_0-\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}B_{t_{k+1}}(g(t_{k+1})-g(t_k))$ up to an endpoint term tending to zero. Brownian path continuity makes the last sums converge pathwise to $\int_0^t g'(s)B_sds$. The $L^2$ limit and this almost-sure limit agree in probability, so $$W_t=e^{\gamma t}B_t-\gamma\int_0^t e^{\gamma s}B_s\,ds$$ almost surely for each fixed $t$. Both sides have continuous versions; equality on rational $t$ holds on one probability-one event and therefore extends to all $t\in[0,T]$. [A1, A2, F2, F3, F4, F5]

1.2 Split the stochastic integral at $s$ and use its linearity: $$X_t=e^{-\gamma(t-s)}X_s+\sigma\int_s^t e^{-\gamma(t-u)}\,dB_u.$$ Step-function approximants to the last deterministic-integrand integral depend only on increments after $s$, so [A1] makes them independent of $\mathcal F_s$. Their $L^2$ limit remains independent of $\mathcal F_s$: for bounded $\mathcal F_s$-measurable $Y$ and bounded continuous $\varphi$, convergence in probability plus boundedness gives convergence of $\mathbb E[Y\varphi(\cdot)]$, preserving the factorization. By [F4] the limit is centered Gaussian; [F3] computes its variance as $\sigma^2\int_s^t e^{-2\gamma(t-u)}du=V(1-e^{-2\gamma(t-s)})$. This proves the conditional transition law and the Markov property. [A1, A2, F3, F4]

2.1 Set $X_t=e^{-\gamma t}X_0+\sigma e^{-\gamma t}W_t$. By [F4] it is continuous and adapted. Step 1.1 rewrites it as $$X_t=e^{-\gamma t}X_0+\sigma B_t-\sigma\gamma\int_0^t e^{-\gamma(t-s)}B_s\,ds.$$ Integrating this continuous expression in $t$, ordinary Fubini [F5] gives $$\int_0^tX_sds=X_0(1-e^{-\gamma t})/\gamma+\sigma\int_0^tB_sds-\sigma\int_0^tB_u(1-e^{-\gamma(t-u)})\,du.$$ Substitution into $X_0-\gamma\int_0^tX_sds+\sigma B_t$ cancels the two $\int B_sds$ terms and leaves exactly the displayed expression for $X_t$. Thus [F1] holds. [A1, A2, F1, F4, F5, step 1.1]

2.2 Taking expectations in the explicit solution, the stochastic integral has mean zero by [F4], giving $\mathbb E X_t=e^{-\gamma t}\mathbb E X_0$. The integral is independent of $X_0$ and centered, so its variance adds to $e^{-2\gamma t}\operatorname{Var}(X_0)$; [F3] evaluates the added variance as $V(1-e^{-2\gamma t})$. The independent Gaussian term tends in law to $N(0,V)$ because its variance tends to $V$ and $e^{-\gamma t}X_0\to0$ in $L^2$; for any bounded continuous test, restrict to a compact interval, use uniform continuity and the second-moment tail bound, then take the interval radius to infinity. [A1, A2, F3, F4, step 1.2]

2.3 Write $r=e^{-\gamma t}$ and $\pi(x)=(2\pi V)^{-1/2}e^{-x^2/(2V)}$. The transition density is $$K_t(x,y)=[2\pi V(1-r^2)]^{-1/2}\exp\!\left(-\frac{(y-rx)^2}{2V(1-r^2)}\right).$$ Multiplying by $\pi(x)$ gives a symmetric prefactor and exponent proportional to $-[x^2+y^2-2rxy]/[2V(1-r^2)]$, unchanged when $x$ and $y$ are exchanged. Hence $\pi(x)K_t(x,y)=\pi(y)K_t(y,x)$, the detailed-balance identity. [A1, A2, F6, F7, step 1.2]

2.4 For $t>0$ let $\mu=e^{-\gamma t}x$, $v=V(1-e^{-2\gamma t})$, and $p(t,x,y)$ be the normal density with mean $\mu$ and variance $v$. Direct differentiation gives $$\partial_t p=p\left(\frac{\mu'(y-\mu)}v+\frac{v'}2\left[\frac{(y-\mu)^2}{v^2}-\frac1v\right]\right),\quad \mu'=-\gamma\mu,\quad v'=\sigma^2-2\gamma v.$$ Also direct $y$-differentiation gives $\gamma\partial_y(yp)+(\sigma^2/2)\partial_{yy}p$ equal to the same expression after writing $y=\mu+(y-\mu)$. Thus $\partial_t p=\gamma\partial_y(yp)+(\sigma^2/2)\partial_{yy}p$. The Gaussian formula has total integral one and converges to point mass at $x$ as $t\downarrow0$; this is the stated positive-time Fokker–Planck solution. [A2, F5, F7, step 1.2]

3.1 If $X$ and $\widetilde X$ are two continuous solutions with the same data, their difference $z$ satisfies $z(t)=-\gamma\int_0^tz(s)ds$. Let $D(t)=\int_0^t|z(s)|ds$. Then $D(0)=0$, $D\ge0$, and $D'(t)=|z(t)|\le\gamma D(t)$ by the equation. The derivative of $e^{-\gamma t}D(t)$ is nonpositive, so this nonnegative function is at most its initial value zero. Hence $D=0$ and continuity gives $z=0$ at every time. [A2, F1, step 2.1, algebra]

3.2 If $X_0$ is centered normal with variance $V$, step 1.2 gives centered Gaussian finite-dimensional laws, since each stochastic integral over a disjoint increment interval is an independent Gaussian and $X_0$ is independent of future increments. Its one-time variance is $V$. For $s\le t$, the split formula in 2.1 and independence of the later increment yield $\mathbb E[X_sX_t]=e^{-\gamma(t-s)}\mathbb E[X_s^2]=Ve^{-\gamma(t-s)}$. Thus covariance depends only on $|t-s|$. A centered Gaussian finite-dimensional law is determined by its covariance matrix; shifting every time by the same amount preserves that matrix and proves stationarity. [A1, A2, F4, step 1.2, step 2.2]

4.1 For $R>0$, the derivative and componentwise FTC in [F6] give $\int_0^R e^{-(\gamma-i\omega)t}dt=(1-e^{-(\gamma-i\omega)R})/(\gamma-i\omega)$. The modulus formula gives $|e^{-(\gamma-i\omega)R}|=e^{-\gamma R}\to0$ and $|e^{-(\gamma-i\omega)t}|=e^{-\gamma t}$, whose integral is finite. Thus the stationary covariance is integrable. By evenness, $$S(\omega)=\frac V\pi\operatorname{Re}\int_0^\infty e^{-(\gamma-i\omega)t}dt =\frac V\pi\operatorname{Re}\frac1{\gamma-i\omega} =\frac{V\gamma}{\pi(\gamma^2+\omega^2)}.$$ The integral converges absolutely because $\gamma>0$. [A2, F6, step 3.2]

5.1 For the stationary time average, Fubini applies to the random product because $\mathbb E|X_sX_t|\le(\mathbb E X_s^2\mathbb E X_t^2)^{1/2}=V$, so its absolute integral over the finite square and probability space is at most $VT^2$. Changing variables in the two triangular halves gives $$\operatorname{Var}\!\left(T^{-1}\int_0^TX_tdt\right) =\frac{2V}{T^2}\int_0^T(T-s)e^{-\gamma s}ds \le\frac{2V}{\gamma T}.$$ The bound tends to zero, so these averages converge to zero in $L^2$ and in probability. It asserts no almost-sure theorem for arbitrary observables. [A1, A2, F5, step 3.2] ∎
